guidance: Calendar reference for Persian dates in correspondence, documents and software, not an official religious or civil announcement. Nowruz in Iran is fixed astronomically, so a year whose equinox falls close to noon can begin a day earlier or later than the arithmetic cycle used here; confirm official holidays against the announced Iranian calendar.
method: Both directions go through one continuous count of days, the day number since 1 January of year 1 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, so the two calendars cannot drift apart and the weekday is simply that count modulo 7. A Solar Hijri year starts at Nowruz, 1 Farvardin, which the arithmetic calendar puts on 20 or 21 March. The year is a leap year of 366 days when (25 x year + 11) mod 33 is less than 8, which places exactly eight leap years in every 33-year cycle (the first, fifth, ninth, thirteenth, seventeenth, twenty-second, twenty-sixth and thirtieth years of the cycle) and leaves the remaining 25 years at 365 days. The page anchors the cycle at 1 Farvardin 1400 = 21 March 2021 and steps whole years from there, adding 365 days plus one for each intervening leap year, so Nowruz walks between 20 and 21 March; the arithmetic rule does not reach 22 March inside the supported window. The first six months, Farvardin to Shahrivar, have 31 days, the next five, Mehr to Bahman, have 30, and Esfand has 29 days, or 30 in a leap year; the day of the Persian year is the fixed-day number minus the Nowruz of that year plus one, and the page also prints the Gregorian date of that Nowruz. The Persian day begins at midnight, unlike the lunar Hijri day that begins at sunset, so the civil weekday and the Persian weekday always agree. Gregorian dates from 1800-01-01 to 2100-12-31 are supported, Persian years 1178 to 1479, and a Persian date whose civil day falls outside that window is refused. Every civil day in the window was compared against ICU's Persian calendar (ca-persian) with no differences, and every date round-trips through the shared day count. The official Iranian calendar fixes Nowruz from the March equinox measured at Tehran, counting the day whose noon follows the equinox, so a year whose equinox falls near noon can differ from the arithmetic rule by one day; this page implements the arithmetic cycle and should be read as a converter rather than an official announcement. Dates must be entered as YYYY-MM-DD, a day beyond the month's length is refused with that length, and a Persian month the chosen year does not have is refused. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
